notes.meaning: A peace offering was a voluntary gift brought to celebrate friendship with God, either to thank him for blessings or to ask for his help. Unlike the burnt offering, this sacrifice could be either a male or a female animal from the herd. The animal had to be completely healthy and without flaw because God always deserves our best.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: The peace offering pictures the Mass, where Christ offers himself so believers can share a sacred meal in communion with God.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Scholars often translate this term as a 'sacrifice of well-being,' emphasizing total peace, health, and wholeness rather than just an end to hostility.

notes.meaning: The worshiper put a hand on the animal's head to transfer ownership to God and name the reasons for prayer or thanksgiving. The animal was then killed right at the entrance of the sacred tent courtyard. The priests threw the blood against all sides of the altar, showing that true peace with God always depends on atonement (being cleansed from sin by blood).

The worshiper removed the fat covering the internal organs, both kidneys with their fat, and the lobe of the liver. The fat was considered the richest part of the animal, while the kidneys and internal organs represented deep feelings and inner life. Giving these specific portions showed that the worshiper was dedicating the very best to God.

The priests burned these fatty parts on top of the daily morning burnt offering that was already on the altar. This showed that prayers of thanksgiving and peace can only be received after sin is first covered by sacrifice. God took delight in this gift, accepting its rising smoke as a pleasing aroma.

If a worshiper chose to bring an animal from the flock instead of a cow or bull, either a male or female was acceptable. Birds could not be used here because they did not provide enough meat or fat for a shared meal. Like every offering, the animal had to be free of any defect to show honor to God.

A person who brought a lamb presented it before the Lord and laid a hand on its head before slaughtering it at the tent entrance. The priests then splashed the blood on all sides of the altar. These repeated actions reminded the worshiper that fellowship with God always requires solemn devotion and the shedding of blood.

Along with the inner fat, kidneys, and liver lobe, the worshiper had to offer the entire fat tail of the sheep cut close to the backbone. The sheep in this region had very large tails filled with rich, fatty marrow that people prized as food. God claimed this choice delicacy for himself, showing that his altar must receive the finest portions first.

The priest burned these pieces on the altar as food offered to the Lord. God does not literally eat food, but the altar served as his table where he shared a symbolic meal with his people. This confirmed that God lived among them and welcomed them as friends into his fellowship.

A worshiper could also bring a goat to present before the Lord. Just as with the other animals, the person laid a hand on its head and slaughtered it, while Aaron's sons sprinkled its blood against the altar. Following these exact steps taught Israel that everyone must approach God with the same obedience and reverence.

The worshiper removed the inner fat around the organs, the two kidneys, and the liver lobe to be burned on the altar. Unlike the sheep, a goat did not have an oversized fat tail, so only the inner fat was burned. God clearly set apart the best separable fat of each animal for his altar.

The priest burned the sacrificial food on the altar as a sweet-smelling gift, declaring that all the fat belongs to the Lord. Because the fat was considered the richest and best part of the animal, God claimed it exclusively for himself. This reminded the people to put God first and not keep the best things only for their own pleasure.

God commanded that no Israelite was ever to eat animal fat or blood, anywhere they lived. The fat belonged to God's altar, and the blood represented the life that makes atonement for sin. This command trained the people in obedience, self-denial, and deep respect for sacred things.

differ.view: The permanent rule against eating blood was tied to the Old Testament sacrificial system and ended when Christ shed his blood on the cross.
Christians should still avoid consuming blood because the apostles in Acts 15 repeated this command for the church.
